source_text: Σὺ δὲ καὶ Ὡς ἐλαία κατάκαρπος ἔσο ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ, μηδέποτε γυμνούμενος τῆς ἐλπίδος, ἀλλ' ἀεὶ θάλλουσαν ἔχων περὶ σεαυτὸν τὴν διὰ πίστεως σωτηρίαν. Οὕτω γὰρ τὸ ἀειθαλὲς τοῦ φυτοῦ μιμήσῃ, καὶ τὸ πολύκαρπον δὲ αὐτοῦ ζηλώσεις, ἄφθονον τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ παρεχόμενος. 5.7 Ἀλλ' ἐπανέλθωμεν πρὸς τὴν ἔρευναν τῶν τεχνικῶν διατάξεων. Πόσα τότε γένη φυτῶν ἐπανέδραμε, τὰ μὲν ἔγκαρπα, τὰ δὲ ἐρέψιμα, ἄλλα πρὸς ναυπηγίαν ἐπιτήδεια, ἄλλα πρὸς καῦσιν; Ἐν τούτοις πάλιν ποικίλη μὲν ἐν ἑκάστῳ δένδρῳ ἡ τῶν μερῶν αὐτοῦ διακόσμησις, δυσέφικτος δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐξεύρεσις τῆς ἑκάστου ἰδιότητος, καὶ ἡ θεωρία τῆς πρὸς ἕκαστον τῶν ἑτερογενῶν διαφορᾶς. Πῶς τὰ μὲν αὐτῶν βαθύρριζα, τὰ δὲ ἀκρόρριζα· καὶ τὰ μὲν ὀρθοφυῆ καὶ μονοστέλεχα, τὰ δὲ χαμαίζηλα καὶ εὐθὺς ἀπὸ τῆς ῥίζης εἰς πολλὰς ἐκφύσεις διῃρημένα. Πῶς ὅσων μὲν οἱ κλάδοι προμήκεις ἐπὶ πολὺ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐκτεταμένοι, τούτων καὶ αἱ ῥίζαι βαθεῖαι, ἐπὶ πλεῖστον ἐν κύκλῳ διανεμόμεναι, οἷον θεμελίους τινὰς ἀναλογοῦντας τῷ βάρει τῶν ἄνωθεν ὑποτιθείσης τῆς φύσεως. Πόσαι τῶν φλοιῶν αἱ διαφοραί; Τὰ μὲν γὰρ λειόφλοια τῶν φυτῶν, τὰ δὲ ῥηξίφλοια· καὶ τὰ μὲν μονόλοπα αὐτῶν, τὰ δὲ πολύπτυχα. Ὃ δὲ θαυμαστὸν, ὅτι καὶ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης νεότητος καὶ τοῦ γήρως εὕροις ἂν καὶ ἐν τοῖς φυτοῖς παραπλήσια τὰ συμπτώματα. Τοῖς μὲν γὰρ νέοις καὶ εὐθαλέσιν ὁ φλοιὸς περιτέταται· τοῖς δὲ γηράσκουσιν οἷον ῥυσοῦται καὶ ἐκτραχύνεται. Καὶ τὰ μὲν κοπέντα ἐπιβλαστάνει· τὰ δὲ μένει ἀδιάδοχα, ὥσπερ τινὰ θάνατον τὴν τομὴν ὑπομείναντα. Ἤδη δέ τινες τετηρήκασιν ἐκτεμνομένας ἢ καὶ ἐπικαιομένας τὰς πίτυς εἰς δρυμῶνας μεθίστασθαι. Τινὰ δὲ καὶ τὴν ἐκ φύσεως κακίαν ἐπιμελείαις γεωργῶν θεραπευόμενα ἔγνωμεν· οἷον τὰς ὀξείας ῥοιὰς, καὶ τῶν ἀμυγδαλῶν τὰς πικροτέρας, ὅταν διατρηθεῖσαι τὸ πρὸς τῇ ῥίζῃ στέλεχος σφῆνα πεύκης λιπαρὸν τῆς ἐντεριώνης μέσης διελαθέντα δέξωνται, εἰς εὐχρηστίαν μεταβάλλουσι τότε τοῦ χυμοῦ τὴν δυσχέρειαν. Μηδεὶς οὖν ἐν κακίᾳ διάγων, ἑαυτὸν ἀπογινωσκέτω, εἰδὼς ὅτι γεωργία μὲν τὰς τῶν φυτῶν ποιότητας μεταβάλλει, ἡ δὲ κατ' ἀρετὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐπιμέλεια, δυνατή ἐστι παντοδαπῶν ἀρρωστημάτων ἐπι κρατῆσαι. Ἡ δὲ περὶ τὰς καρπογονίας διαφορὰ τῶν καρπίμων φυτῶν τοσαύτη, ὅσην οὐδ' ἂν ἐπελθεῖν τις δυνηθείη τῷ λόγῳ. Οὐ γὰρ μόνον ἐν τοῖς ἑτερογενέσιν αἱ διαφοραὶ τῶν καρπῶν, ἀλλ' ἤδη καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ εἴδει τοῦ δένδρου πολὺ τὸ διάφορον· ὅπουγε καὶ ἄλλος μὲν χαρακτὴρ τοῦ καρποῦ τῶν ἀρρένων, ἄλλος δὲ τῶν θηλειῶν, παρὰ τῶν φυτουργῶν διακέκριται, οἵ γε καὶ τοὺς φοίνικας εἰς ἄρρενας καὶ θηλείας διστῶσι. Καὶ ἴδοις ἄν ποτε τὴν παρ' αὐτῶν ὀνομαζομένην θήλειαν, καθιεῖσαν τοὺς κλάδους, οἷον ὀργῶσαν, καὶ τῆς συμπλοκῆς ἐφιεμένην τοῦ ἄρρενος, τοὺς δὲ θεραπευτὰς τῶν φυτῶν ἐμβάλλοντας τοῖς κλάδοις, οἷόν τινα σπέρματα τῶν ἀρρένων, τοὺς λεγομένους ψῆνας, καὶ οὕτως οἷον ἐν συναισθήσει τῆς ἀπολαύσεως γίνεσθαι καὶ ἀνορθοῦσθαι πάλιν τοὺς κλάδους, καὶ πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον σχῆμα τοῦ φυτοῦ τὴν κόμην ἀποκαθίστασθαι. Τὰ αὐτὰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ περὶ τῶν συκῶν φασιν.
thought_title: The olive tree, the variety of plants, and the moral lesson of cultivation
orientation: Basil is addressing his congregation, drawing moral lessons from the plant world as he continues his exposition of the third day of creation.
pass_a_gloss: But you, be as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, never being stripped of hope, but always having around yourself the salvation through faith flourishing. For thus you will imitate the evergreen quality of the plant, and you will emulate its fruitfulness, providing almsgiving abundantly at every season. But let us return to the investigation of the technical arrangements. How many kinds of plants sprang up then, some fruit-bearing, some for roofing, others suitable for shipbuilding, others for burning? In these again, varied is the arrangement of the parts in each tree, and difficult to attain is the discovery of the peculiarity of each, and the contemplation of the difference toward each of the different kinds. How some of them are deep-rooted, others shallow-rooted; and some are straight-growing and single-stemmed, others are low-growing and immediately from the root divided into many shoots. How, for as many as the branches are long, stretched out far into the air, for these also the roots are deep, distributed in a circle to the greatest extent, as if nature lays down certain foundations corresponding to the weight of the things above. How many are the differences of the barks? For some of the plants are smooth-barked, others are cracked-barked; and some of them are single-layered, others many-folded. And what is wonderful, that you would find also in plants symptoms similar to those of human youth and old age. For in the young and flourishing ones the bark is stretched tight; but in the aging ones it is as it were wrinkled and roughened. And some, when cut, sprout again; but others remain without successors, as if enduring the cutting as a kind of death. And already some have observed that pines, when cut out or even burned over, change into thickets. And we have known some that are healed of their natural badness by the care of farmers; for example, the sharp pomegranates, and the bitterer of the almonds, when, having been bored through, the trunk near the root receives a rich wedge of pine driven through the middle of the pith, they change then the unpleasantness of the juice into usefulness. Let no one therefore living in wickedness despair of himself, knowing that cultivation changes the qualities of plants, but the care of the soul according to virtue is able to overcome all kinds of infirmities. And the difference concerning the fruit-production of the fruit-bearing plants is so great, as not even one could go through in speech. For not only among the different kinds are the differences of the fruits, but already even in the very species of the tree there is much difference; since indeed one is the character of the fruit of the males, another of the females, distinguished by the plant-growers, who also divide the palms into males and females. And you might see at some time the one called female by them, letting down the branches, as if in heat, and desiring the intertwining with the male, and the tenders of the plants throwing into the branches, as it were certain seeds of the males, the so-called gall-insects, and thus as if in consciousness of the enjoyment it happens and the branches are straightened again, and the foliage is restored to the proper shape of the plant. And these same things they say also about the fig trees.

choices.term: Ὡς ἐλαία κατάκαρπος ἔσο ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ
choices.english: Be as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God
choices.why: The imperative force of ἔσο is preserved; κατάκαρπος rendered as 'fruitful' to match the olive-tree image from the Psalm
rejected: Be like a fruit-laden olive tree
Be as an olive tree bearing fruit

choices.why: The passive participle with genitive of separation is rendered literally to keep the sense of being deprived or denuded of hope
The prepositional phrase διὰ πίστεως is kept as 'through faith' to preserve the Pauline sense of faith as the means of salvation
The adjective denotes plants used for thatching or roofing; rendered as a purpose adjective to match the parallel 'for shipbuilding' and 'for burning'

choices.term: οἷον θεμελίους τινὰς ἀναλογοῦντας τῷ βάρει τῶν ἄνωθεν ὑποτιθείσης τῆς φύσεως
choices.english: as if nature lays down certain foundations corresponding to the weight of the things above
choices.why: The simile with οἷον and the genitive absolute with ὑποτιθείσης is rendered fully to preserve the causal and comparative force
rejected: as if nature placed foundations proportionate to the weight above
like foundations laid by nature for the weight above

choices.term: ὥσπερ τινὰ θάνατον τὴν τομὴν ὑπομείναντα
choices.english: as if enduring the cutting as a kind of death
choices.why: The accusative θάνατον with the participle is rendered as 'as a kind of death' to preserve the appositional force of τινὰ
rejected: as if suffering death by the cutting
as though the cutting were death

pass_b_english: And you, be as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, never being stripped of hope, but always keeping the salvation through faith flourishing around you. For in this way you will imitate the evergreen quality of the plant, and you will also rival its abundance of fruit, offering generous almsgiving at every season. But let us return to the investigation of the skilled arrangements. How many kinds of plants sprang up then—some bearing fruit, some for roofing, others suitable for shipbuilding, others for burning? In these again, the arrangement of each tree's parts is varied, and the discovery of each one's particular character is hard to attain, as is the observation of its difference from each of the other kinds. How is it that some of them are deep-rooted and others shallow-rooted, and some grow upright with a single stem, while others are low-growing and immediately divided from the root into many shoots? How is it that those whose branches stretch far out into the air also have deep roots, spreading widely in a circle, as if nature places certain foundations beneath, corresponding to the weight of the things above? How many are the differences of the barks? For some plants are smooth-barked, others cracked-barked; and some of them have a single layer of bark, others many folds. And what is wonderful is that you would find in plants symptoms closely resembling those of human youth and old age. For in the young and flourishing the bark is stretched tight around them, but in those that grow old it becomes wrinkled, as it were, and rough. And some, when cut, sprout again; but others remain without successors, as if enduring the cutting as a kind of death. Indeed, some have observed that pines, when cut down or even burned over, turn into oak forests. And we know that some trees are cured of their natural badness by the care of farmers—for example, the sharp pomegranates and the more bitter almonds, when their trunk near the root is pierced and they receive a greasy wedge of pine driven through the middle of the pith, then change the unpleasantness of their juice into usefulness. Let no one, then, who lives in wickedness despair of himself, knowing that farming changes the qualities of plants, and the care of the soul according to virtue is able to overcome all kinds of infirmities. And the difference in the fruit-bearing of fruit trees is so great that no one could even cover it in speech. For not only are there differences of fruit among the different kinds, but even within the very species of a tree there is much variation; indeed, the growers distinguish one character of fruit for the male trees and another for the female, and they divide even the palms into male and female. And you might at some time see the one they call female letting down her branches, as if in heat, and longing for the embrace of the male; and the tenders of the plants cast into the branches, as it were, certain seeds of the males, the so-called gall-insects, and so she becomes, as it were, aware of the enjoyment, and her branches straighten up again, and her foliage is restored to the proper shape of the plant. They say the same things also about the fig trees.

problems.why: λιπαρὸν modifies the wedge (accusative), not 'pine'; 'rich' is odd for a wedge—'oily' or 'greasy' (from resin) is meant
problems.ruling: λιπαρὸν 'oily/resinous' modifies σφῆνα; 'rich' loses the resinous sense the context requires.

problems.why: ὀργῶσαν means 'swelling/teeming/fertile' (of plants), not 'in desire' which anthropomorphizes sexually; it's botanical terminology
problems.ruling: ὀργῶσαν 'swelling/aroused' is botanical; 'in desire' over-sexualizes, misleading readers on plant imagery.

fixed: Changed 'a rich wedge of pine' to 'a greasy wedge of pine': λιπαρὸν modifies σφῆνα (the wedge), meaning 'oily/greasy' from resin, not 'rich'.
Changed 'as if in desire' to 'as if swelling with fertility': ὀργῶσαν is botanical terminology meaning 'swelling/teeming/fertile', not sexual desire.

problems.quote: as if nature lays down certain foundations
problems.source_quote: οἷον θεμελίους τινὰς ἀναλογοῦντας τῷ βάρει τῶν ἄνωθεν ὑποτιθείσης τῆς φύσεως
problems.why: ὑποτιθείσης is present participle, 'laying/putting underneath,' but the syntax shows nature is the subject laying foundations corresponding to weight above; 'lays down' misses that nature actively places them beneath as support.
problems.fix: as if nature places certain foundations beneath, corresponding to the weight above

problems.why: ὀργῶσαν means 'in heat/estrus/rut' (sexual excitement of animals), extended metaphorically to plants; 'swelling with fertility' loses the explicit sexual connotation crucial to the pollination metaphor that follows.
problems.ruling: ὀργῶσαν means 'in heat/rut'; 'swelling with fertility' loses the sexual connotation central to the pollination metaphor.

problems.quote: And the difference in the fruit-bearing of fruit trees
problems.source_quote: Ἡ δὲ περὶ τὰς καρπογονίας διαφορὰ τῶν καρπίμων φυτῶν τοσαύτη, ὅσην οὐδ' ἂν ἐπελθεῖν τις δυνηθείη τῷ λόγῳ
problems.why: Missing 'so great' (τοσαύτη) and 'that' (ὅσην...ὅτι construction); the English loses the exclamatory 'so great that no one could cover it' emphasis.
problems.fix: And the difference in the fruit-bearing of fruit trees is so great that no one could even cover it in speech
problems.ruling: τοσαύτη...ὅσην ('so great that') is omitted; English drops the exclamatory force and correlative structure.

edits.old: as if nature lays down certain foundations corresponding to the weight of the things above
edits.new: as if nature places certain foundations beneath, corresponding to the weight of the things above

edits.old: And the difference in the fruit-bearing of fruit trees is so great that no one could even cover it in speech.
edits.new: And the difference in the fruit-bearing of fruit trees is so great that no one could even cover it in speech.

fixed: Changed 'lays down' to 'places certain foundations beneath' to reflect the active, supportive sense of ὑποτιθείσης (nature placing foundations underneath).
Changed 'swelling with fertility' to 'in heat' to capture the explicit sexual connotation of ὀργῶσαν, which is crucial to the pollination metaphor.
The English already includes 'so great' and 'that' from τοσαύτη and the ὅσην...ὅτι construction; no edit needed.

last_rejected.why: ὀργῶσαν means 'swelling' or 'budding,' not 'in heat'; botanically wrong and introduces sexual arousal sense alien to source.
last_rejected.ruling: ὀργῶσαν can mean 'swelling with desire/heat'; 'in heat' is within range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: συναίσθησις here means 'shared perception/sensation' (of pollination), not 'awareness of enjoyment'; anthropomorphizes plant sexuality misleadingly.
last_rejected.fix: as if sharing in the sensation of receiving
last_rejected.ruling: συναίσθησις can mean 'perception/sensation'; 'awareness of enjoyment' captures the anthropomorphic οἷον adequately.

last_rejected.why: ψῆνες are 'fig-wasps' or 'gall-wasps,' specific pollinators; 'gall-insects' is too broad and misses the technical agricultural term.
last_rejected.ruling: ψῆνας denotes gall-wasps; 'gall-insects' is a reasonable rendering, not a meaning change or loss.
